pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, with numbers and named trade-offs rather than component lists; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through a URL shortener end to end — key generation, storage, the redirect path, and analytics — and defend one choice in each of those four areas.
expected_points: key generation: random plus conditional insert with retry, or a counter handed out in ranges, with the collision or coordination cost named
storage: a single-key lookup, hash-partitioned by key, with read replicas or a KV store — chosen by access pattern and operations, not fashion
redirect path: cache the hot set, expect a high hit rate, negative-cache misses, and consider edge locations for cross-ocean latency
analytics: emit an event to a queue and aggregate asynchronously; never write click rows on the redirect path
each defended by a requirement, with the alternative and its cost named

questions.prompt: For a chat system, explain how you handle connections, message fan-out, per-conversation ordering, and delivery to someone who was offline.
expected_points: long-lived connections on a thin gateway tier plus a session registry; polling is ruled out by arithmetic
the durable log is the commit point and delivery is best-effort; fan-out on write for small conversations, read from the shared log for very large ones
ordering from a per-conversation sequence number assigned by one owner — partition by conversation, never sort by timestamps
offline delivery as sync from a per-device cursor, with client-generated message ids for deduplication and bounded catch-up

questions.prompt: A prompt lands: 'design a system that shortens links'. What do you do first, second, third — and how do you decide what to go deep on?
expected_points: requirements and scope first, functional split must/nice plus non-functional targets and an out-of-scope list
estimation second, ending in a named dominant axis
high-level design third, walking one or two flows end to end, every box tied to a requirement
deep dives chosen by the estimate — the dominant axis picks them, not taste
bottlenecks and evolution last; loop back and amend earlier phases when a deep dive changes them

questions.prompt: Take either design you built and answer as if I were interviewing you: what breaks first at 10x the load, and what do you do about it?
expected_points: checks the drill: singleton, hot key or partition, unbounded growth, synchronous fan-out, coordination point
names one specific component of their own design, not a generic layer
names the first symptom they would see on a dashboard
names the next evolution step and what that step costs — complexity, money, staleness, or operational load

questions.prompt: Links become editable and a takedown must take effect globally within 60 seconds. Which parts of the immutable-link design stop working, and what replaces them?
expected_points: the invalidation-free cache is gone: entries can now be stale, so TTLs and purges become load-bearing
301 becomes unusable because browsers and proxies cache it beyond your reach; 302 or 307 plus no-store headers
a purge is best-effort, so a TTL ceiling is needed as the backstop that bounds worst-case staleness
the tighter the propagation rule, the shorter the TTL and the higher the origin load — that is the trade-off to state

questions.prompt: Two chat products have nearly identical feature lists but very different architectures. Give me the non-functional requirements most likely to explain that, with the design consequence of each.
expected_points: concurrent connection count decides whether the gateway tier is a handful of boxes or hundreds
retention and searchability decide storage tiering and cost, and attachments can dominate text by orders of magnitude
residency or compliance rules force regional partitioning of content and constrain what may be global
latency and ordering guarantees decide the partitioning key and whether coordination is needed at all
